---
title: "Semantic plots"
subtitle: "Why plots stay live inside Flux — the fluxplot contract"
---

Most tools treat a saved plot as a picture. Flux treats it as a **structure**: when a plot is
made with [fluxplot](https://github.com/fluxsci/fluxplot), every meaningful part of it — a
series' line, its 4th data point, the x-axis title — carries a **stable name**. That one idea is
what makes Flux figures feel alive:

- **Click into a plot and restyle a part** — one line's color, one label's size — in
  [Figure mode](../modes/figure.qmd), without touching your analysis code.
- **Regenerate without losing your tuning.** Re-run the analysis script and the plot updates in
  place; your per-part restyles survive, because they're keyed to the part *names*, not to
  pixels.
- **Animate at the level of parts** in [Slide mode](../modes/slide.qmd) — fade one series in,
  draw a curve on, morph one chart into another.

# What fluxplot is

`fluxplot` is an ordinary Python library you use in your analysis environment — "matplotlib,
but every meaningful thing has a name." You plot through thin helpers that take a series name,
then save with `fp.save()`:

```python
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import fluxplot as fp
from fluxplot import style as fx
fx.use_light()                       # the house style (Flexoki palette, clean look)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.8))
fp.line(ax, t, control,   series="control",   marker="o", label="Control")
fp.line(ax, t, treatment, series="treatment", marker="s", label="Treatment")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (h)"); ax.set_ylabel("OD600"); ax.legend()

fp.save(fig, "plots/growth.svg",
        recipe=dict(script=__file__, params=p, inputs=["data/growth.csv"]))
```

Saving into your project's `plots/` folder writes **three files that travel together**:

```
plots/growth.svg            ← the plot, with named, addressable parts
plots/growth.fluxplot.json  ← the manifest: data, coordinates, parts inventory
plots/growth.recipe.json    ← the recipe: how it was made, so it can be re-made
```

Name series consistently across related plots: the name is the handle Flux restyles by.
When saving from a Python script, fluxplot discovers the script automatically. Pass
`recipe={"script": __file__, "params": p, "inputs": [...]}` when you need explicit parameters
and input provenance; `recipe=False` suppresses script discovery. The full API and style guide
ship with fluxplot itself; setup is covered in [Installation](../installation.qmd).

# True physical size

Plots import at their **true printed size**: a matplotlib `figsize=(6.4, 4.8)` panel lands on
the canvas at exactly 6.4 × 4.8 inches, and what you lay out is what prints. Flux never silently
rescales an import to fit — if a plot is bigger than its figure frame, it overflows visibly
(with a toast pointing at **Ctrl+Shift+I** to bring it inside). Sizing decisions belong to you
and your plotting code, not to an importer.

# Regenerate, don't re-save

To change a plot, **re-run the script** rather than hand-editing the output. With the app open,
the regenerated plot hot-swaps into your figures live, restyles intact. And because the recipe
records the script, its parameters, and its inputs, a plot can be regenerated *with different
parameters* — from the app or the command line — without editing code.

# What about plots from anywhere else?

Other SVGs also import with an automatically derived parts tree for editing and animation;
PNGs remain images. Derived SVG parts do not carry the original scientific data or a recipe.
Fluxplot supplies that additional meaning. (If a
fluxplot-saved plot imports as a flat image, something's wrong — `flux validate-plot
plots/<name>.svg` says what.)

# Multiple panels and precise data

Fluxplot schema 0.3 keeps each subplot's series and axes separate, including shared axes,
twins and insets. Give panels stable names before plotting when their layout may change:

```python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, layout="constrained")
fp.panel(axes[0], "baseline")
fp.panel(axes[1], "followup")
```

Both panels can now use `series="control"` without merging their identities. Ordinary single-panel
plots retain their existing part names. Saving after editing captures the current artist data;
small scientific values keep their precision, and missing observations remain gaps.

Slides use each series' owning axes when interpolating data. A matching line/scatter plot with
supported linear or logarithmic axes can morph in data space. Polar/3D projections, unsupported
scales, field layers and other composite plots use the complete transition behavior. Existing
projects stay readable; upgrading does not regenerate your plots automatically.

# Matrices, contours and color scales

Use `fp.heatmap`, `fp.contour`, `fp.contourf` and `fp.colorbar` to name the field and its key:

```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
image = fp.heatmap(ax, matrix, series="correlation", cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=1)
fp.colorbar(image, name="correlation", label="Correlation")
fp.save(fig, "plots/correlation.svg")
```

For a modest matrix, `cells=True` makes individual cells addressable. Large fields stay efficient
as one named raster layer. Raw matrix values are only included when `include_values=True`.

With fluxplot 0.3.1 or later the saved plot records each colour scale's exact law — the colormap
table, the normalisation and its limits — and every coloured element's data value, so Flux
recolours the plot itself. Select the plot and edit **Colour scales** in the Object inspector, or
**colour scale** in its **F** menu: the palette, its direction, the norm kind, the limits and
`extend` change live, together with the colorbar, and the edit is saved with the figure or slide
and tweens in a talk. **Apply to source** writes the complete colour controls into the recipe
(`__fluxplot__`, keyed by the series name) and regenerates the plot from source data while
preserving your named-part overrides; the plot needs a runnable recipe, and the action targets
that plot's save, leaving sibling outputs untouched. Plots saved before 0.3.1 keep the
regenerate-only palette and range fields in **X-Ray**.

The same manifest carries each series' **colour** (its hex and, when fluxplot drew it from a
palette, the exact token) and every scaffold element's **theme token**, so Flux can give a whole
series one colour — **Series colour** in the Plot part section, `set-series-color` headless — and
let a slide plot **follow the deck theme** (its ink, axes and gridlines take the theme's colours;
data colours never move). Reading a figure's data is a verb, not a squint: `get-plot-data`
returns every series' exact values and per-point ids, hexmatrix bins, glowbar / fluxbox
statistics, heatmap values, image channels, axis domains and each significance bracket's test and
p, windowing long arrays; hovering a part with **Ctrl** held shows the same facts on the canvas.

New imports and linked-source reloads verify the SVG/manifest checksum before accepting the
bundle. If generation is still writing files or the sidecar belongs to another SVG, Flux keeps
the last accepted plot and reports the mismatch. This check precedes any legacy SVG repair.
